title: What Is Wrong With the Prosperity Gospel?
subtitle: On prosperity, platform, and the church that learned to worship winning
question: What happens to a faith built on a crucified man when it starts measuring itself by attendance, revenue, reach, and the size of the stage?
whyItMatters:
The prosperity gospel is the easiest heresy to mock and the hardest to escape. We point at the man on television promising a private jet and we feel clean, because we would never say it that crudely. But the gospel of success is wider than its loudest salesmen. It is the quiet conviction that God blesses the impressive, that growth proves favor, that the church doing well is the church getting bigger. It lives in the language of the smallest plant church and the largest denominational office. It is the water we swim in.

I have preached for fifteen years, and I have felt it in my own chest. The relief when the numbers were up. The unspoken sense that a full room meant God was pleased and an empty one meant I had failed Him. That is the prosperity gospel in pastoral form, and no one ever caught me preaching it because I never said it out loud. The worship of winning does not need a doctrine. It only needs a heart that already wants to win, and a culture that already calls winning blessed.
biblicalFoundation:
Jesus did not recruit the way we build. He said to take up a cross and follow, and a cross was not a metaphor for a hard season. It was an instrument of public execution, and everyone listening knew exactly what it meant. The first beatitude does not bless the strong. It blesses the poor in spirit, the ones who arrive with nothing in their hands, the ones with no platform and no claim on God. The kingdom is theirs. That is the foundation, and it is built downward.

Paul asked three times to have his thorn removed, and three times the answer was no. The reply he received is the sentence that undoes the entire gospel of bigness: my power is made perfect in weakness. Not displayed despite weakness. Perfected in it. Paul then says he will boast in his weaknesses, which is the opposite of every platform built on a highlight reel. The apostle who planted churches across an empire measured his ministry by his scars, not his reach.

The pastoral letters press it further. Godliness with contentment is great gain, Paul writes to Timothy, and then warns that those who want to get rich fall into a trap and many griefs. This is not a footnote. It is a direct collision with a theology that reads wealth as evidence of favor. And behind all of it stands the servant of Isaiah, the one who had no beauty or majesty that we should desire him, no form that would draw a crowd. The center of our faith is a man the marketing department would have rejected.

Then there is the warning we skip. Woe to you who are rich, Jesus says, for you have already received your comfort. The man who tore down his barns to build bigger ones, certain that bigger was wiser, heard God call him a fool that very night. Scripture does not treat success as neutral. It treats it as a spiritual danger sharp enough to require its own warnings, because the thing that looks like blessing is the thing most likely to replace the One who blesses.

churchRecord.led: At its best the church has named this idol from inside its own walls. The early martyrs refused to call Caesar lord even when conformity was the path to safety and status. Monastic movements walked away from wealth on purpose. Bonhoeffer wrote against cheap grace from a country where the church had traded the cross for the flag, and he paid for the sentence with his life. Wherever the church has chosen the small, the hidden, and the costly over the impressive, it has told the truth about its Lord.
churchRecord.failed: And at its worst the church has baptized the empire it was meant to confront. After Constantine it learned to love proximity to power, and it has rarely unlearned it since. We built sanctuaries to rival palaces. We measured pastors by the size of their buildings and platforms, and we made celebrity a spiritual gift. The prosperity preachers are not an alien intrusion into the American church. They are its most honest mirror. They simply said out loud what the rest of us were quietly counting.

whereWeAgree: Almost everyone can see the crude version. Few defend the private jet, and most believers across the political map agree that faith is not a vending machine for wealth. The trouble is not that we disagree about the obvious lie. It is that we each keep a respectable version of it.
captureLeft: On the left the success gospel wears the robes of relevance and influence. It measures a church by its cultural standing, its platform on the right issues, its seat at the tables that matter, and it quietly treats being admired by the powerful and the educated as the proof that the gospel is working.
captureRight: On the right it is more familiar and more frank. Bigger is blessed, growth is favor, and the full parking lot and the rising budget become the evidence that God is with us, until the size of the operation becomes indistinguishable from the smile of God.
whereWeDiffer: One side wants the approval of the cultured despisers and the other wants the rewards of the market, but both have agreed that the church should be winning by a scoreboard the world already keeps. The cross keeps a different scoreboard, and it is not one either party wants to read aloud.
theCost: To preach against the gospel of success is to indict your own ministry, because the metrics that flatter you are the ones you must repent of. It means telling a growing church that growth is not proof of anything, and telling a shrinking one that smallness is not failure. It means losing the comfort of the numbers, and standing before God without the scoreboard you have been hiding behind. I do not write this from above it. I write it as a man still learning to want the right things.
charge: Go and look honestly at what makes your chest swell on a Sunday. If it is the size of the room, the reach of the platform, the sense that you are winning, then you have found the idol, and it has your name on it. The crucified servant had no beauty that we should desire him. Follow Him anyway, downward, toward the cross you were told to carry and not to escape.

right.label: Prosperity, platform, and the church measured by its size
right.whatItLooksLike: On the right the gospel of success speaks plainly about wealth, health, and increase as the visible proof of God's favor. A full auditorium, a rising budget, a pastor with a recognizable brand and a publishing deal become the working evidence that God is present and pleased. The crude version promises a healing or a financial breakthrough in exchange for a seed offering, and the respectable version simply assumes that growth is vindication.
right.inThePast: The lineage runs through the New Thought currents of the late nineteenth century and into the post war healing revivals, where figures like Oral Roberts built ministries around seed faith giving and the promise of physical and financial return. Kenneth Hagin systematized the Word of Faith teaching, and Kenneth Copeland carried it onto television and into a global broadcast ministry. The 1980s televangelism boom, and the 1987 to 1989 collapse of the PTL ministry under Jim Bakker, exposed how far the equation of wealth with blessing had traveled. Kate Bowler's history Blessed traces this as a distinctly American theology rather than a fringe accident.
right.now: Today the teaching reaches mass audiences through broadcast and online ministries associated with figures who have stated these views publicly, including Creflo Dollar, who in 2015 solicited donations toward a Gulfstream jet, and Joel Osteen, whose Lakewood Church fills a former sports arena in Houston. The wider current is the megachurch measured by attendance and the pastor measured as a personal brand, documented in reporting on church planting metrics, multisite expansion, and conference circuits. The same logic surfaced in scandals at large churches such as Mars Hill in Seattle and at Hillsong, where institutional growth and celebrity leadership were later examined as the very pressures that broke them.

left.label: Relevance, influence, and the platform as the measure of a ministry that matters
left.whatItLooksLike: On the left the success gospel trades the private jet for cultural cachet, measuring a ministry by its standing among the admired and the educated. The proof of favor becomes being on the right side of history, holding a platform on the issues that signal seriousness, and earning a seat at the tables the culture respects. It rarely names money as the prize, which is exactly what makes it easier to keep.
left.inThePast: The pattern has older roots in the early twentieth century Social Gospel and in the mainline Protestant assumption that respectability and progress went together, a confidence Reinhold Niebuhr criticized for overestimating its own righteousness. The mid century alliance between Protestant establishment and cultural prestige gave the church proximity to power that it read as relevance. The emergent church conversation of the 2000s, associated with figures like Brian McLaren, reframed faithfulness partly as cultural credibility and being heard by skeptics.
left.now: Now the measure is platform itself, documented in the rise of the influencer pastor and the Instagram ministry where reach and follower count function as currency. The deconstruction movement and a wave of celebrity progressive Christian voices have built large audiences on Substack, podcasts, and social media, where being quoted approvingly by mainstream outlets reads as proof that the message is working. The same scoreboard runs through the platform and creator church economy, where conference invitations, book deals, and verified accounts confer the authority that attendance once did.
